transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-09-14 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~46 min
Attendees: Alex (Redwood AE), Samira (Redwood SE), Jordan (CedarPark CTO), Priya (Lead ML Eng), Mark (Infra), Pat (PM)

[00:00] Alex (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intros?
[00:05] Jordan (CedarPark): Jordan here, CTO, Priya's my lead on ML, Mark handles infra, Pat product. We want to understand how fast we can get to first token and what hosting options make sense given our compliance needs.
[00:18] Alex: Great. The goal for today is to cover TTFT for the PLG self-serve path with credits, and map when you'd pivot to dedicated or private. Samira will do a quick tech run-through.
[00:30] Samira (Redwood SE): Hi all, quick outline: hosted quickstart flow, common blockers (network, auth, model selection), and an example runbook to TTFT.
[00:40] Priya (CedarPark): We're building a contextual chat assistant inside our support product. Key non-negotiables: P95 latency under 550ms for 512-token inference, audit logs for prompt/response retention for 1 year, and SSO for access. Also, we may need EU data residency.
[00:58] Samira: Ok noted. Hosted can meet P95 depending on model/seq length; we recommend starting with a smaller sequence sample to validate. Our hosted API gives you free credits for a pilot to get TTFT.
[01:12] Pat: How long to hit TTFT? From signup to first successful request — like a measurable runbook.
[01:20] Alex: Typical flow for PLG self-serve is minutes to register, minutes to install SDK/Postman, then a couple steps to paste a prompt set. In previous pilots we've had teams hit first token in under 20 minutes, realistic expectation ~15-60 minutes depending on infra and firewall rules.
[01:38] Jordan: Firewall rules and egress are the sticking point for us. Mark, can you chime in?
[01:43] Mark (Infra): We do strict outbound whitelisting, need IPs or domain names. Also VPC peering might be required for on-prem calls. We prefer redwood to support VPC peering for later stages.
[01:54] Samira: For quickstart you can also use SDK via public API — we provide a list of endpoints and a short-lived key. If egress is blocked you'll need to allow a CIDR set or temporary tunnel. We'll send the exact endpoints.
[02:10] [02:10] Priya: On the model side, what would you recommend for chat? And cost-wise, tradeoffs?
[02:17] Samira: We usually start with a mid-sized open model variant — it's a balance between cost and latency. For P95 under 550ms on a 512 token window, smaller quantized models on our hosted fleet often hit that. If you need lower latency or higher concurrency, reserved Dedicated instances are better.
[02:33] Alex: Also mention caching — we have prefix/KV cash caching (note: 'KV cash' typo in transcription) that can dramatically reduce tail latency for repeated prompts.
[02:41] Priya: Can caching be used with private deployments?
[02:44] Samira: Yes, both Dedicated and Private support the same runtime features; only difference is where the control plane lives and networking.
[02:52] [03:00] Jordan: Security — we need SOC2 type II, SSO SAML (or OIDC), KMS/HSM integration, and full audit logs.
[03:12] Alex: We have SOC2, SSO via SAML and OIDC, KMS integrations, and per-request audit logging. For Private we can put the control plane in your VPC and integrate with your KMS.
[03:25] Mark: For Private, what's the upgrade path? We might begin hosted for dev then move to private for prod. How disruptive is that?
[03:33] Samira: It's designed to be low-friction: same API surface and SDKs. You can pin model versions and rollout policies. The main lift is networking and key provisioning.
[03:42] Priya: About data retention: we need to ensure we can opt-out of any analytics retention by Redwood for pilot.
[03:48] Alex: For enterprise accounts we can disable retention of request/response payloads; for hosted pilots we keep minimal telemetry but can sign an addendum for non-retention during the pilot. We'll share the privacy checklist.
[03:59] [04:10] Pat: How do credits get applied? Do they expire? What can they be used for?
[04:16] Alex: Pilot credits are applied to the account, usually valid for 90 days, usable for text generation/embeddings. We'll allocate a small pool to run your tests.
[04:25] [04:30] Priya: We need to run simple perf tests: 1) single-request latency at steady-state, 2) small burst (10qps), 3) long conversation traces to understand context window throughput.
[04:42] Samira: Good set. We'll provide a sample script and Postman collection. Also we'll propose a small benchmarking matrix: models x batch sizes x concurrency.
[04:54] Jordan: Competitors — we've previously looked at MajorCloudAI and OpenServe. Their managed endpoints felt like black boxes; we want more observability. How much per-token visibility do you provide?
[05:06] Alex: Token-level cost and latency breakdown per route/model in Redwood Console, and tracing hooks you can add to your traces.
[05:14] Priya: Great. Also ask about function calling — we plan to call internal microservices to enrich responses. Does Redwood support structured function outputs?
[05:23] Samira: Yes, streaming responses and tool/function calling are supported. There can be edge cases when you're in private on-prem where streaming requires additional proxy config — we'll note that in the runbook.
[05:36] [05:40] Jordan: Any immediate red flags for TTFT?
[05:44] Samira: The usual are network egress, API key provisioning policies, and long-running SSO provisioning. For TTFT under an hour, ask infra to allow outbound to our endpoints and one admin to create an account.
[05:54] Pat: For the first-run UX, will a non-engineer PM be able to run the Postman script to hit first token?
[06:00] Alex: Yes, we design the quickstart to be non-engineer friendly; Postman or simple curl works. We'll include screenshots.
[06:08] Priya: Any model warmup recommended?
[06:11] Samira: For high P95 you can use small warmup traffic or cached prefixes. Warmup helps KV cache priming.
[06:20] [06:40] Jordan: Let's talk timeline: We're aiming to land a pilot and evaluate within 2 weeks. Is that feasible?
[06:45] Alex: Yes — pilot via hosted quickstart using credits should be doable in <=2 weeks. If you need dedicated capacity that's a longer process (2-6 weeks for provisioning depending on commit). Private is a few weeks to months depending on networking and compliance scans.
[06:58] Mark: For Dedicated, what's autoscaling behavior and cost predictability?
[07:03] Samira: Dedicated pools have reserved capacity with configurable autoscaling policies and burst capacity; pricing is commit-based. We'll share the Dedicated one-pager.
[07:12] Priya: We may want to run a small dedicated test if we see latency variability on hosted. Would we be able to test a single reserved node?
[07:19] Samira: Yes, we can do a limited dedicated eval with a short-term commit in some cases. We'll explore that after the pilot.
[07:27] [07:40] Jordan: Observability — will we get per-prompt logs, error breakdowns, and traces for tokenization issues?
[07:48] Alex: Console provides per-route/per-model dashboards, error traces, and tokenization insights. We can also stream logs to your SIEM via webhook or direct export for enterprise accounts.
[07:59] Priya: For compliance audits we need exportable audit logs for a year.
[08:04] Alex: We'll include that in the security checklist — exportable and immutable logs are supported for enterprise/private.
[08:13] [08:30] Pat: Any gotchas with SSO?
[08:34] Samira: SAML config sometimes requires exchange of certs and test users; that'll delay quickstart if SSO is enforced for the pilot. Consider a time-limited API key for the pilot.
[08:44] Mark: We can't have broad-scoped API keys in prod but for pilot we can set a short lived key.
[08:49] Alex: We'll recommend a limited-scope key and rotate after pilot.
[08:53] [09:20] Priya: Regarding EU residency — can hosted allocate regional instances in eu-west?
[09:25] Samira: Yes, hosted has EU regions. For strict residency with no data leaving EU you may need a Private deployment or a dedicated EU-only cluster; we can advise based on your retention and audit needs.
[09:38] Jordan: Ok. Next, cost modeling — we need a rough estimate for 1M tokens/month across chat and embeddings.
[09:46] Alex: We'll ship a model-cost matrix in the spreadsheet Samira will prepare; depends on batching, model, and embeddings footprint. Expect a 2-4x variance between smallest and largest models.
[09:58] [10:10] Pat: Can we run a quick example now?
[10:14] Samira: We could do a quick demo but probably better to send the Postman and have you try with your prompts.
[10:20] Jordan: Sounds good.
[10:22] Alex: To recap next steps: we'll send TTFT runbook, a Postman collection, allocate pilot credits, and schedule a perf scoping session with Mark and Priya.
[10:33] Priya: We'll share 50 prompt examples and P95 targets.
[10:37] Mark: I'll confirm network constraints.
[10:40] Alex: Anything else?
[10:43] Pat: No. Thanks.
[10:45] Alex: Great, we'll follow up with the checklist. Thanks everyone.

End of transcript.

Notes on transcription quality: some speaker overlaps, occasional mis-heard words ("KV cash"), and punctuation errors.
